decks.title: Final Accounts of Companies — Part 1: Schedule III, Heads and Classification
goals: State what Section 129 and Schedule III Part I of the Companies Act, 2013 require of a company Balance Sheet
Name the major heads and sub-heads of Equity and Liabilities and of Assets in order, including the amended captions
Decide whether an asset or a liability is current or non-current using the operating cycle and the twelve-month rule
Classify the balances of a company and draw up its Balance Sheet with notes

slides.heading: Final Accounts of Companies
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **form** of a company Balance Sheet under **Schedule III Part I**, its **heads and sub-heads**, and how to **classify** every balance. Every company, person and figure in this chapter is imagined.

nodes.label: Section 129 and Schedule III Part I
Equity and Liabilities: heads and sub-heads
Assets: heads and sub-heads
Current or non-current?
A complete Balance Sheet with notes

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the law that fixes the form, the heads and sub-heads of equity and liabilities and of assets, the test for current and non-current items, and a complete balance sheet with notes
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A company must present its Balance Sheet in a form fixed by law, so that every reader finds each item in the same place. In this part we learn that form, the major heads and sub-heads of Schedule Three, Part One, the test that separates current from non-current items, and the recent changes in captions. Our running company is Thoseghar Agri Drones of Satara.

slides.heading: What the law and the ISC syllabus ask for
slides.body_md: For ISC 2027 the **Statement of Profit and Loss (Part II) is not required** for final accounts: profit is given, or found in one working.

rows: Financial statements must give a true and fair view and follow the form in Schedule III
Form of the Balance Sheet: vertical; Equity and Liabilities first, then Assets
Form of the Statement of Profit and Loss: **not required** for ISC 2027 final accounts
The details behind each figure, numbered and quoted against it on the face of the Balance Sheet
A Balance Sheet with notes from a trial balance and adjustments; profit given or found in a working

visual.alt: Table of the rules behind company final accounts: section one hundred and twenty-nine requires a true and fair view in the form of Schedule Three; Part One gives the vertical balance sheet; Part Two, the statement of profit and loss, is not required for the ISC final accounts; notes give the details; the ISC question asks for a balance sheet with notes from a trial balance and adjustments

slides.narration: Section one hundred and twenty-nine of the Companies Act requires financial statements that give a true and fair view, in the form set out in Schedule Three. Part One of that schedule gives the form of the Balance Sheet. Your syllabus asks for the Balance Sheet with notes, prepared from a trial balance with adjustments. The Statement of Profit and Loss in Part Two is not required.

slides.heading: The form: Equity and Liabilities
slides.body_md: Four major heads, always in this order; each sub-head carries a **note number** when it needs details.

rows: (a) Share Capital; (b) Reserves and Surplus; (c) Money Received against Share Warrants
(a) Long-term Borrowings; (b) Deferred Tax Liabilities (Net); (c) Other Long-term Liabilities; (d) Long-term Provisions
(a) Short-term Borrowings; (b) Trade Payables; (c) Other Current Liabilities; (d) Short-term Provisions

visual.alt: Table of the equity and liabilities part of Schedule Three: shareholders funds with share capital, reserves and surplus and money received against share warrants; share application money pending allotment as a head by itself; non-current liabilities with long-term borrowings, deferred tax liabilities, other long-term liabilities and long-term provisions; current liabilities with short-term borrowings, trade payables, other current liabilities and short-term provisions
visual.caption: Schedule III Part I: I. Equity and Liabilities

slides.narration: The first part of the Balance Sheet shows where the money came from. Shareholders funds come first, then share application money pending allotment as a head of its own, then non-current liabilities and finally current liabilities. Learn the sub-heads in order, because the examiner expects them in exactly this sequence.

slides.heading: The form: Assets
slides.body_md: The amended caption is **Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets**, with four sub-heads.

rows: (a) Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets: (i) Property, Plant and Equipment, (ii) Intangible Assets, (iii) Capital Work-in-Progress, (iv) Intangible Assets under Development; (b) Non-current Investments; (c) Deferred Tax Assets (Net); (d) Long-term Loans and Advances; (e) Other Non-current Assets
(a) Current Investments; (b) Inventories; (c) Trade Receivables; (d) Cash and Cash Equivalents; (e) Short-term Loans and Advances; (f) Other Current Assets

visual.alt: Table of the assets part of Schedule Three: non-current assets with property, plant and equipment and intangible assets (property, plant and equipment, intangible assets, capital work-in-progress and intangible assets under development), non-current investments, deferred tax assets, long-term loans and advances and other non-current assets; current assets with current investments, inventories, trade receivables, cash and cash equivalents, short-term loans and advances and other current assets
visual.caption: Schedule III Part I (as amended): II. Assets

slides.narration: The second part shows how the money is used. Non-current assets come first. Their first group, after the amendment, is property, plant and equipment and intangible assets, with four sub-heads: property, plant and equipment, intangible assets, capital work in progress and intangible assets under development. Current assets follow, from current investments down to other current assets.

slides.heading: Current or non-current?
bullets: The **operating cycle** runs from buying inputs to collecting cash from customers.
When no single cycle can be identified, Schedule III takes a cycle of **twelve months**.

nodes.label: Will the item be realised or settled within the normal operating cycle?
Is it held mainly for trading?
Is it due within twelve months after the Balance Sheet date?
Yes to any question: current. No to all: non-current

visual.alt: Flow of the test for current items: an asset or liability is current if it will be realised or settled within the normal operating cycle, or is held mainly for trading, or is due within twelve months after the balance sheet date; otherwise it is non-current
visual.caption: A liability is also current if the company cannot put off paying it for twelve months.

slides.narration: An item is current if it will be realised or settled within the normal operating cycle, if it is held mainly for trading, or if it falls due within twelve months after the Balance Sheet date. Everything else is non-current. Remember that a long operating cycle can make an item current even when it is more than a year away.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: classifying Thoseghar’s liabilities
slides.body_md: Thoseghar Agri Drones Ltd, Satara (imagined), on 31 March 2026. Place each liability under its major head and sub-head.

rows: Term loan instalment due in January 2027
Provision for gratuity payable after twelve months

visual.alt: Table classifying eight liabilities of Thoseghar Agri Drones: the debentures under long-term borrowings, the loan instalment due within a year and the overdraft under short-term borrowings, bills payable under trade payables, the customer advance and accrued interest under other current liabilities, the gratuity provision under long-term provisions and the tax provision under short-term provisions
visual.caption: Thoseghar Agri Drones Ltd, Satara (imagined), 31 March 2026.

slides.narration: Take each liability in turn. The debentures run to twenty thirty, so they are long-term borrowings. The loan instalment due next January and the overdraft are short-term borrowings. Bills payable are trade payables. The customer advance and the accrued interest are other current liabilities. The gratuity provision is long-term and the tax provision short-term.

slides.heading: Quick check: no clear operating cycle
slides.body_md: Fill in the number.
slides.narration: Recall the length that Schedule Three assumes when a company cannot identify its normal operating cycle.

slides.heading: Shareholders' Funds and the separate head
slides.body_md: Owners’ money stays together; money still **owed back** to shareholders does not.

rows: Shareholders' Funds: subscribed capital less calls in arrears, plus forfeited shares not reissued (note)
Securities premium, capital reserve, general reserve
Surplus, i.e. balance in the Statement of Profit and Loss
Last line of Reserves and Surplus; a debit balance is shown negative there
Share application money pending allotment (not refundable)
A major head by itself, after Shareholders' Funds
Not capital: Current Liabilities, Other Current Liabilities

visual.alt: Table of where shareholders' items go: share capital net of calls in arrears plus forfeited shares; reserves including the surplus, which may be negative; money against share warrants; share application money pending allotment as a head by itself; calls in advance as an other current liability

slides.narration: Shareholders funds hold share capital, reserves and surplus, and money received against share warrants. Share capital is shown net of calls in arrears, plus forfeited shares not yet reissued. Share application money that will not be refunded sits as a separate head. Calls received in advance are not capital at all: they are other current liabilities.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: Thoseghar’s Equity and Liabilities
slides.body_md: Thoseghar has 1,20,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, fully paid (authorised 2,00,000 shares), and the balances classified in worked example 1.

visual.alt: Equity and liabilities part of Thoseghar's balance sheet: share capital 12,00,000, reserves and surplus 5,30,000, long-term borrowings 7,40,000, long-term provisions 70,000, short-term borrowings 1,10,000, trade payables 2,50,000, other current liabilities 57,500 and short-term provisions 90,000, total 30,47,500
visual.caption: Thoseghar Agri Drones Ltd (imagined): I. Equity and Liabilities as at 31 March 2026. Notes are in worked example 5.

slides.narration: Here is the first part of Thoseghar's Balance Sheet. Shareholders funds total rupees seventeen lakh thirty thousand. Non-current liabilities, the long-term borrowings and the gratuity provision, come to rupees eight lakh ten thousand. Current liabilities add rupees five lakh seven thousand five hundred. Each sub-head with more than one item gets a note number.

slides.heading: Quick check: four liabilities, four sub-heads
slides.body_md: Match each liability with its sub-head.
slides.narration: Ask of each liability whether it is a borrowing, a provision or another kind of liability, and whether it is due within the year.

slides.heading: Assets: captions after the amendment
slides.body_md: Finished assets in use and assets **still being built or developed** are kept apart.

rows: Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets

visual.alt: Table of the amended captions for fixed assets: fixed assets became property, plant and equipment and intangible assets; tangible assets became property, plant and equipment; intangible assets, capital work-in-progress and intangible assets under development are the other three sub-heads
visual.caption: The amendment also renamed "Securities Premium Reserve" as "Securities Premium" (Reserves and Surplus).

slides.narration: The amended Schedule Three renamed fixed assets as property, plant and equipment and intangible assets. Tangible assets are now called property, plant and equipment. An asset still under construction is capital work in progress, and an intangible still being developed has its own line. The same amendment renamed securities premium reserve as simply securities premium.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: classifying Thoseghar’s assets
slides.body_md: Eight of Thoseghar’s assets on 31 March 2026, each placed under its sub-head.

rows: Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets: Property, Plant and Equipment
Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets: Intangible Assets
Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets: Capital Work-in-Progress
Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets: Intangible Assets under Development
Advance paid for a moulding press

visual.caption: Thoseghar Agri Drones Ltd (imagined), 31 March 2026.

slides.narration: Thoseghar owns plant, which is property, plant and equipment. Its flight-control software is an intangible asset, but the crop-mapping software still being written is an intangible under development. The hangar being built is capital work in progress. The advance for a press is a long-term advance, the drone kits are inventories and the bills are trade receivables.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: Thoseghar’s Assets
slides.body_md: Cash at bank of ₹3,22,500 completes the list of assets.

rows: (a) Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets

visual.alt: Assets part of Thoseghar's balance sheet: property, plant and equipment 13,80,000, intangible assets 1,10,000, capital work-in-progress 1,50,000, intangible assets under development 60,000, non-current investments 1,00,000, long-term loans and advances 40,000, inventories 5,10,000, trade receivables 3,30,000, cash and cash equivalents 3,30,500, short-term loans and advances 25,000 and other current assets 12,000, total 30,47,500
visual.caption: Thoseghar Agri Drones Ltd (imagined): II. Assets as at 31 March 2026.

slides.narration: The assets side follows the same order every time. Property, plant and equipment of rupees thirteen lakh eighty thousand comes first, with the other fixed-asset lines beside it. Current assets end with cash and other current assets. The total is rupees thirty lakh forty-seven thousand five hundred, exactly the total of equity and liabilities.

slides.body_md: True or false?

slides.body_md: Money raised (left) = money used (right).

slides.heading: Worked example 5: Thoseghar’s notes to accounts
slides.body_md: The figures on the face of the Balance Sheet come from these notes.

rows: Authorised capital: 2,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each
Issued capital: 1,20,000 equity shares of ₹10 each
Subscribed and fully paid: 1,20,000 equity shares of ₹10 each
Surplus, i.e. balance in the Statement of Profit and Loss
Term loan from a bank (excluding the instalment due in January 2027)
Term loan instalment due in January 2027

visual.alt: Notes to accounts of Thoseghar, numbered one to 10: share capital 12,00,000, reserves and surplus 5,30,000, long-term borrowings, short-term borrowings, trade payables, other current liabilities, property, plant and equipment, inventories, trade receivables, cash and cash equivalents and other current assets
visual.caption: Thoseghar Agri Drones Ltd (imagined): notes to accounts as at 31 March 2026.

slides.narration: Each note lists the items behind one figure on the face of the Balance Sheet and ends with the same total. Share capital shows the authorised and issued capital for information. Borrowings separate the debentures from the loan. Plant is shown at cost less accumulated depreciation, and debtors less the provision for doubtful debts.

slides.heading: Quick check: shareholders' funds
slides.body_md: Owners’ money only.
slides.narration: Deduct calls in arrears from share capital, deduct the debit balance within the reserves, and leave the debentures out.

slides.heading: Classification traps

rows: Deducted in the Share Capital note
Debit balance of the Statement of Profit and Loss
Negative item in Reserves and Surplus

visual.alt: Table of eight classification traps: calls in advance, calls in arrears, loose tools, premium on redemption, a capital advance, debentures due within a year, proposed dividend and a debit balance of profit and loss, each with its correct place and the usual mistake

slides.narration: These eight items cause most of the lost marks. Calls in advance are a liability, while calls in arrears are deducted in the share capital note. Loose tools are inventories. The redemption premium is a long-term liability. A debit balance of profit and loss stays inside reserves and surplus as a negative figure, and the proposed dividend is only a note.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Schedule III Part I: Equity and Liabilities, then Assets; totals on the face, details in notes
Operating cycle, held for trading, or due within 12 months: current
Share capital, reserves and surplus (may be negative), share warrants
Borrowings, other liabilities and provisions, each long-term or short-term
Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets first; current assets last
Both parts must total the same

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the form of Schedule Three, the current and non-current test, shareholders funds, liabilities and assets by sub-head, and the check that both parts agree

slides.narration: To sum up: Schedule Three, Part One fixes the order of heads and sub-heads. Test each item against the operating cycle, trading and the twelve-month rule. Shareholders funds come first, then liabilities. Property, plant and equipment and intangible assets open the assets side. Put the details in notes and make sure both parts agree.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the heads and sub-heads **in Schedule III order**, with a Note No. column.
Give the **major head and the sub-head** for every item you classify: half marks are lost for the sub-head alone.
Remember the amended captions: **Property, Plant and Equipment**, **Securities Premium**, **Intangible Assets under Development**.
Never show a loss or calls in arrears as an asset.
Total both parts and check they agree before moving on.
slides.narration: In the exam, write the heads and sub-heads in their legal order with a column for note numbers. When you classify an item, give both the major head and the sub-head. Use the amended captions. Never show a loss or unpaid calls as an asset. And total both parts before you move on: a difference tells you something is misplaced.

Prepare the Balance Sheet of a company from a trial balance with adjustments

slides.heading: Notes to Accounts and the Balance Sheet from a Trial Balance
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the **notes** behind each figure, the **adjustments** and the **profit working**, and a complete Balance Sheet from a **trial balance**.

nodes.label: Notes to accounts
Share Capital note
Profit working and Reserves and Surplus
Borrowings and current maturities
Fixed assets and receivables
Proposed dividend: contingent

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: notes to accounts, the share capital note, the profit working with reserves and surplus, borrowings with current maturities, fixed assets and receivables, and the proposed dividend as a contingent liability
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: A board final-accounts question gives you a trial balance and a list of adjustments, and asks for the Balance Sheet with notes. In this part we build the notes one at a time: share capital, reserves and surplus, borrowings, and fixed assets, and we see where each adjustment goes. Our running company is Kunchikal Rainwear of Agumbe.

slides.heading: Notes to accounts
slides.body_md: The face of the Balance Sheet shows **one figure per sub-head**; the **note** shows how it is made up.

nodes.label: Trial balance and adjustments
Numbered notes (the details)
Balance Sheet (one figure per sub-head, with its note number)
Contingent liabilities: disclosed, not added

visual.alt: Flow from the trial balance and adjustments to numbered notes, then to the balance sheet which shows one figure per sub-head with its note number, and finally contingent liabilities which are disclosed but not added
visual.caption: How notes and the Balance Sheet fit together

slides.narration: Notes to accounts carry the details that would clutter the face of the Balance Sheet. Each note is numbered, and its number is written against the figure it explains. A note ends with the same total as that figure. Items that are only possible obligations, such as a proposed dividend, are disclosed in a note but never added in.

slides.heading: The note on Share Capital
slides.body_md: Only **subscribed** capital is added; authorised and issued capital are information.

rows: Shares taken up and fully paid
Amount called up, less calls in arrears
Amount received on forfeited shares not yet reissued

visual.alt: Table of the share capital note: authorised and issued capital shown for information only; subscribed and fully paid capital, subscribed but not fully paid capital net of calls in arrears, and forfeited shares not reissued are added to the total

slides.narration: The share capital note begins with the authorised capital and the issued capital. These are shown for information and are not added. The total is the subscribed capital: shares fully paid, plus shares not fully paid at their called-up amount less calls in arrears, plus the amount received on forfeited shares that have not yet been reissued.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: Kunchikal’s Share Capital
slides.body_md: Kunchikal Rainwear Ltd (imagined) is authorised to issue 1,50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each. It issued 1,00,000; 1,000 were forfeited after ₹4 per share had been paid and are not reissued; the other 99,000 are fully paid.

rows: Authorised capital: 1,50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each
Issued capital: 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each
Subscribed and fully paid: 99,000 equity shares of ₹10 each
Add: Forfeited shares (amount paid on 1,000 shares)

visual.alt: Share capital note of Kunchikal Rainwear: authorised 15,00,000, issued 10,00,000, subscribed and fully paid 9,90,000, plus forfeited shares 4,000, total 9,94,000
visual.caption: Kunchikal Rainwear Ltd, Agumbe (imagined): 1,000 shares forfeited earlier (₹4 per share received) are not reissued.

slides.narration: Authorised and issued capital are listed first. The ninety-nine thousand shares in the hands of shareholders are fully paid. The four thousand rupees received on the forfeited shares is added. The note totals rupees nine lakh ninety-four thousand, the figure shown against share capital.

slides.heading: Quick check: share capital with arrears and forfeiture
slides.body_md: Deduct what is unpaid; add back what was forfeited.
slides.narration: Start from the subscribed capital, take away the calls in arrears and add the amount received on the forfeited shares.

slides.heading: Reserves and Surplus: where the profit lands
slides.body_md: Surplus = opening balance + profit for the year − transfers to reserves.

nodes.label: Profit for the year (given, or found in a working)
Surplus: opening balance + profit
Less: transfer to General Reserve
Closing surplus in Reserves and Surplus

visual.alt: Flow of the profit into reserves: the profit for the year is added to the opening surplus, the transfer to general reserve is deducted, and the closing surplus is shown in reserves and surplus
visual.caption: A proposed dividend is not deducted: it is only disclosed.

slides.narration: The profit for the year is added to the surplus brought forward. Any transfer to general reserve is taken out of the surplus and added to the reserve, so the total of reserves and surplus does not change. If the surplus is a debit balance, it is shown as a negative figure inside reserves and surplus.

slides.heading: Adjustments: each one is posted twice

rows: Added to accumulated depreciation, deducted in the PPE note

visual.alt: Table of nine adjustments with their effect on profit and the balance sheet line they change: depreciation, provision for doubtful debts, outstanding and prepaid expenses, interest accrued, provision for tax, transfer to general reserve, current maturities and proposed dividend
visual.caption: Each adjustment that changes the profit also changes exactly one other line, so the Balance Sheet still agrees.

slides.narration: Every adjustment in a final-accounts question touches two places. Depreciation lowers the profit and raises the accumulated depreciation. An outstanding expense lowers the profit and becomes a current liability. A prepaid expense raises the profit and becomes a current asset. Transfers, debentures falling due and a proposed dividend do not touch the profit at all.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: Kunchikal’s trial balance
bullets: Depreciate buildings at 5% and plant and machinery at 10% on cost.
Keep the provision for doubtful debts at 5% of debtors.
Wages of ₹14,000 are outstanding; insurance of ₹6,000 is prepaid.

sections.heading: 1. Company final accounts and Schedule III Part I
sections.body_md:
Under **Section 129** of the **Companies Act, 2013**, a company's financial statements must give a **true and fair view** and be drawn up in the form of **Schedule III**. **Part I** of the Schedule gives the form of the **Balance Sheet** (vertical: I. Equity and Liabilities, then II. Assets), with **notes to accounts**; Part II gives the form of the Statement of Profit and Loss.

**ISC 2027 scope:** the Balance Sheet as per Schedule III Part I with notes to accounts, prepared from a **trial balance with adjustments**. *Not in the ISC 2027 syllabus:* the Statement of Profit and Loss as per Schedule III Part II is not required for final accounts, so the profit for the year is either given or worked out in one simple working.

**Layout of the face:** Particulars | Note No. | amount at the year end (the previous year's figures are shown alongside in practice).

sections.heading: 2. Current and non-current items
sections.body_md:
**Operating cycle:** the time between acquiring the materials for processing and collecting the cash for the finished goods. If a normal operating cycle cannot be identified, Schedule III assumes twelve months.

**An asset is current** when it is expected to be realised (or sold or consumed) in the normal operating cycle, is held mainly for trading, is expected to be realised within twelve months after the reporting date, or is cash or a cash equivalent that is not restricted.

**A liability is current** when it is expected to be settled in the normal operating cycle, is held mainly for trading, is due within twelve months after the reporting date, or the company cannot defer its settlement for at least twelve months.

Everything else is **non-current**. A long operating cycle (aged rice, maturing timber) can make an item current although it is more than a year away.

key_terms.definition_md: The time from buying inputs for processing to realising cash from customers.
A liability settled within the operating cycle or due within twelve months after the reporting date.

sections.heading: 4. Notes to accounts: the Share Capital note

sections.heading: 8. Recent amendments and contingent liabilities
sections.body_md:
The ISC 2027 syllabus lists these amended Schedule III points:
1. **Proposed dividend:** not a liability until the shareholders declare it at the annual general meeting; it is not provided for and is shown under **contingent liabilities and commitments** in the notes.
2. **Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets** replaces "fixed assets: tangible / intangible".
3. **Current maturities of long-term borrowings** are shown under **Short-term Borrowings**.
4. **Securities Premium** (formerly "Securities Premium Reserve") is shown under Reserves and Surplus.

**Note: Contingent Liabilities and Commitments (to the extent not provided for)** — for example a proposed dividend, claims against the company not acknowledged as debts, guarantees given. The amounts are disclosed, not added.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving only the major head (or only the sub-head) when asked to classify.
- Adding authorised or issued capital to the share capital total; forgetting to deduct calls in arrears or to add forfeited shares.
- Showing calls in advance in Share Capital, or loose tools under Property, Plant and Equipment.
- Using the old provision for doubtful debts instead of the required one, or deducting only this year's depreciation.
- Leaving debentures or loan instalments due within twelve months in Long-term Borrowings.
- Providing for a proposed dividend or deducting it from the surplus.
- Showing a debit balance of the Statement of Profit and Loss as an asset.

**How marks are usually awarded (SOYL chapter tests on the ISC default pattern)**
- 1 mark: objective items.
- 2 marks: classifying four items (half a mark each, in pairs), one short note, or a rule with an example.
- 3 marks: one note with workings (share capital, reserves, borrowings, fixed assets) or six classifications.
- 5 marks in parts, e.g. (a) 3 + (b) 2: notes and the Balance Sheet, or a working and a note.
- Full practical (practice, 8 marks): profit working about 2, notes about 4, the Balance Sheet with totals and the contingent note about 2. The ISC 2027 weightage for Final Accounts of Companies in Paper I is 7 marks.

**Figures in SOYL practice** are imagined; your board paper will give its own.

questions.stem_md: Barehipani Honey Ltd, an imagined company at Jashipur, paid its last dividend in September 2025, but dividend warrants for ₹3,200 had not been encashed by 31 March 2026. The ₹3,200 is shown under

Shareholders' Funds — Reserves and Surplus
Current Liabilities — Other Current Liabilities
Current Liabilities — Trade Payables

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Current Liabilities — Other Current Liabilities. It is a definite sum owed to known shareholders and payable on demand: an other current liability, not an estimate (provision) and not an amount owed to suppliers.

questions.stem_md: Kempty Teak Boats Ltd, an imagined boat-builder near Mussoorie, seasons teak planks before they go into a hull; its normal operating cycle is 22 months. Planks bought in February 2026 will be used in about 16 months. In the Balance Sheet as at 31 March 2026 the planks are

options.text_md: a current asset under Inventories, as they will be used within the normal operating cycle
a non-current asset, as they will be used after more than twelve months
Capital Work-in-Progress, as the boats are not yet built
a non-current investment, as seasoned teak gains in value

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a current asset under Inventories, as they will be used within the normal operating cycle. Non-current Liabilities — Long-term Provisions

under Other Current Liabilities
under Reserves and Surplus

questions.stem_md: Dabbe Aged Basmati Ltd, an imagined rice mill at Sagara, stores paddy for about fourteen months before milling and selling it; its normal operating cycle is sixteen months. On 31 March 2026 it has: (a) aged rice in its godowns that will be sold in fifteen months; (b) money owed to farmers for paddy, payable in thirteen months as part of the usual crop-to-cash cycle; (c) a bank loan for a new silo, repayable in one sum in fourteen months. Classify each item as current or non-current, with the sub-head and a reason.
questions.solution_md: Items inside the operating cycle are tested against the cycle; the loan, outside it, against the twelve-month rule.

answer.model_answer_md:
- **(a) Aged rice:** to be sold within the normal operating cycle of sixteen months, so it is a **current asset** under Inventories, although the sale is more than twelve months away.
- **(b) Amount owed to farmers:** expected to be settled within the normal operating cycle, so it is a **current liability** under Trade Payables.
- **(c) Silo loan:** a borrowing that is not part of the operating cycle; it is due after more than twelve months, so it is **non-current**, under Long-term Borrowings.

questions.stem_md:
Pandavkada Bakery Ovens Ltd, an imagined company at Kharghar, is preparing its Balance Sheet as at 31 March 2026.

(a) State the major head and the sub-head of each of the following balances: (i) Bills payable to flour suppliers; (ii) Ovens under installation in a new bakery unit; (iii) Provision for tax for the year; (iv) Recipe software bought from a developer; (v) Interest accrued on 8% debentures; (vi) Security deposit paid to the landlord of the bakery. [3]

(b) The company also owes a bank ₹5,00,000 on a term loan repayable in five equal yearly instalments, the next one on 15 February 2027. Show how the loan is presented, and explain the rule you applied. [2]
questions.solution_md: Part (a) classifies item by item; part (b) splits the loan at the twelve-month line.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)**

| Item | Major head | Sub-head |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bills payable to flour suppliers | Current Liabilities | Trade Payables |
| Ovens under installation in a new bakery unit | Non-current Assets | Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets: Capital Work-in-Progress |
| Provision for tax for the year | Current Liabilities | Short-term Provisions |
| Recipe software bought from a developer | Non-current Assets | Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets: Intangible Assets |
| Interest accrued on 8% debentures | Current Liabilities | Other Current Liabilities |
| Security deposit paid to the landlord of the bakery | Non-current Assets | Long-term Loans and Advances |

**(b)** Each instalment is ₹5,00,000 ÷ 5 = ₹1,00,000. The instalment due on 15 February 2027 falls within twelve months of the Balance Sheet date, so ₹1,00,000 is shown under **Current Liabilities — Short-term Borrowings** as current maturities of long-term borrowings; the remaining ₹4,00,000 stays under **Non-current Liabilities — Long-term Borrowings**. questions.solution_md: Both are possible obligations that depend on a future event; disclose each with its amount.

Amboli Jackfruit Papad Ltd, an imagined company at Sawantwadi, issued 10,000 11% debentures of ₹100 each at par in 2023, redeemable at a premium of 5%: 2,000 debentures on 31 January 2027 and the rest in 2030. The full premium on redemption was credited to Premium on Redemption of Debentures Account when the debentures were issued. Interest is paid on 30 September and 31 March; the interest due on 31 March 2026 was still unpaid on that date.

(a) Prepare the extract of the Equity and Liabilities part of the Balance Sheet as at 31 March 2026 with the notes for these items. [3]

(b) Explain the two presentation rules of the amended Schedule III that you applied to the debentures. [2]
questions.solution_md: Split the debentures at twelve months, keep the redemption premium as another long-term liability, and record the unpaid interest as a current liability.

(b) The accountant wants to deduct the proposed dividend from the surplus. Explain why this is wrong and how the dividend is shown. [2]
